title: Reliance after effort
hookLine: trust after effort: the tied camel

lines: A MAN, A CAMEL, A QUESTION.
cards: Shall I tie it, or shall I trust? A man asks the Prophet ﷺ about his camel, and it sounds almost like a riddle. Should he tie up his camel and rely on Allah, or leave it loose and rely on Allah?
If you truly trust, why bother with a rope? And if you bother with a rope, are you really trusting? The answer, recorded in the collection of al-Tirmidhi, is short.
Tie it, and trust. Today, the station that lives in that and.

teach.b: The station is tawakkul, reliance on Allah. The tied camel shows its shape: effort first, then trust, and neither cancels the other.

The Qur'an puts the order plainly, speaking to the Prophet about consulting his companions, in Pickthall's translation: "And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah. Lo! Allah loveth those who put their trust (in Him)."
Consult, think, decide, then trust. Another picture in al-Tirmidhi is easy to misread.
The Prophet said that if people relied on Allah as He should be relied on, He would provide for them as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry and come back in the evening full.
Some hear that as, sit still and food will come. But the birds go out. They fly all day.
The trust is in the going out, not instead of it. So there are two ways to miss tawakkul. One is the loose camel: doing nothing and calling it faith.
You tie the camel, then tie it again, then sit up all night watching the knot.
That's effort with no trust in it, and it's exhausting.
Tawakkul is the step after the knot. You've done what a sensible person does. The result was never in your hands.
So you hand it over, and you sleep. Gratitude used the gift well; reliance uses effort well, then lets go of what effort can't reach.

how: Muslims teach tawakkul as trust in Allah that follows real effort, and the saying 'tie your camel and trust' is a common way of reminding someone to do their part before leaving the result to Allah.

o: leaving everything to fate, without making any effort
tawakkul: doing your part, then trusting Allah with the rest
a vow to Allah to do a good deed if a prayer is answered

games.q: the tied camel — tap the pairs.
p: go out hungry, come back full

s: real tawakkul means leaving the camel untied
the answer was: tie it, and trust. effort first.
in the Qur'an, trust comes after resolving on a decision
"when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah."
the birds in the hadith wait in their nests for food
they go out hungry in the morning and come back full. the trust is in the going out.

games.q: you have a camel, and you ask the Prophet ﷺ: should you tie it and trust Allah, or leave it loose and trust Allah? what does he say?
o: leave it loose. that's real trust.
tie it, and stay beside it all night.
games.why: in al-Tirmidhi's collection the answer is short: tie it, and trust. effort and reliance go together.

practice: Bring up one thing you're worried about, a test, a payment, a conversation, someone's health, and ask the camel question: what's the one sensible rope within your reach, and when will you tie it?
Then look at what's left over, the outcome, other people's choices, and let your hands open on your knees, as if setting that part down.
If you pray, you can say hasbunallah, Allah is enough for us; if not, just breathe out and leave it there.

wordCard.voice: Reliance after effort. Tawakkul: doing what is yours to do, then trusting Allah with what was never in your hands. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: reliance, trust, handing a matter over to Allah.

carryVoice: Your line: tie it, trust him. Tie the rope, then let the knot be. Until tomorrow.
